claims.locator: Commit object format: tree, parent commits if any, author/committer, blank line, message
claims.rationale: The object text lists tree, parents, author, committer, a blank line, and the message. Rewriting History says a changed message rewrites that commit and all descendants. The supplement reworded only the oldest commit, kept the tree, and changed all five ids. Those page sentences are nonblank-identical on this head.

claims.locator: Book heading “Don’t push your work until you’re happy with it”, rewrite.txt derived lines 323-328 and 376. Pushed work is treated as final, and line 376 says an already-pushed rewritten commit confuses other developers. The manual heading RECOVERING FROM UPSTREAM REBASE is rebase.txt line 1849 and is not in this book extract.
claims.rationale: Lines 323-328 say local history can be rewritten until it is pushed, and pushed work should be treated as final. Line 376 says not to include a commit already pushed to a central server, because other developers then see an alternate change. The page's coordination requirement and merge-or-revert default for shared history follow that warning. Additional manual support is rebase snapshot sha256:b6dfb34be8e8c71f6b0418b7edb2af7da620957c7d8ac358582cfac79b9ab02b at derived line 1849: rebasing a branch others have based work on forces downstream history repair. The prior locator attached that manual heading to the book URI. The book extract does not contain it. The page sentences are unchanged.

claims.locator: FAST-FORWARD MERGE when HEAD is an ancestor of the named commit; TRUE MERGE creates a commit with both parents
claims.rationale: Fast-forward moves HEAD without a merge commit. Otherwise the merge commit has both branches as parents. The supplied fast-forward had a parent word count of 2. The supplied diverged --no-ff merge had a parent word count of 3.

claims.locator: DESCRIPTION: list equivalent-filtered commits, detach at upstream, replay one by one, then move the branch; stop at the first conflict
claims.rationale: Replay is one commit at a time and stops with conflict markers. Resolution is git add and git rebase --continue. The detached checkout in that sequence supports the page's detached-HEAD conflict statement.

claims.locator: INTERACTIVE MODE example: git rebase -i HEAD~5 and move the first patch; book says the sheet lists the oldest at the top
claims.rationale: The manual's linear example uses HEAD~5 to reorder the latest five commits. The book says the sheet is the reverse of git log and is executed from top to bottom. rewrite.txt line 422 says it lists the oldest at the top.

claims.locator: pick = use commit; reword = use commit, but edit the commit message; descendants of a changed message are rewritten
claims.rationale: A picked commit is replayed. A message change creates a new object, and later commits that name the new parent change too. The page says the pick id can change, which leaves room for the unchanged-pick reuse case.

claims.locator: INTERACTIVE MODE: squash melds into the previous commit and opens the combined messages; fixup is squash that discards this commit's log message
claims.rationale: The book shows the combined-message editor. Git 2.56.0 captured a two-commit squash template containing both subjects, and the resulting message kept both. The page does not teach fixup -c or fixup -C.

claims.locator: SPLITTING COMMITS: mark edit, git reset HEAD^, stage, commit, repeat, then git rebase --continue
claims.rationale: Edit stops after applying the commit. The manual says the result need not remain one commit. rebase.txt lines 1799-1842 contain SPLITTING COMMITS, edit, reset, HEAD^, add, commit, and rebase --continue, with the command broken across derived lines. The supplied edit stop printed the amend and continue instructions, and the split sequence ran reset, two commits, and continue.

claims.locator: DESCRIPTION: default mode is --mixed; working directory unchanged and index reset so nothing is staged
claims.rationale: git reset HEAD~1 without a mode is mixed. HEAD and the index move, and the worktree stays. The page's following git add commands match that unstaged index. The splitting section describes the same HEAD^ effect.

claims.locator: Deleting a commit: drop, or delete the line; removing a line means that commit will be lost from the replay
claims.rationale: The comment block says removing a line drops that commit from the rewritten branch. The supplied drop removed ingress.yaml from the branch tip. The reflog section is the recovery path, not a promise that the object remains forever.

claims.locator: INTERACTIVE MODE exec: the command runs in a shell and a non-zero status stops the rebase; --exec inserts it after each commit
claims.rationale: The manual says a failing exec stops the rebase until --continue. Git 2.56.0 stopped on exec false with execution failed, then --continue left a clean tree. A successful exec test -f file5 completed in the earlier run.

claims.locator: DESCRIPTION conflict handling: mark resolved files with git add, then git rebase --continue
claims.rationale: The manual's ordinary conflict path is add and continue, not a separate user commit. The page reserves git commit for an edit pause where the user is amending or replacing the stopped commit.

claims.locator: MODE OPTIONS --abort resets HEAD to the starting branch; --quit leaves index and working tree unchanged
claims.rationale: Abort returns to the pre-rebase branch. The quit contrast shows abort does not leave the index and worktree as they were mid-conflict. The book says the repository returns to the state from before the rebase. The supplied abort restored the saved feature tip.

claims.locator: DESCRIPTION records hand resolutions and reapplies them; the index is left alone for a later diff and git add; reuse holds while the recorded resolution is still applicable
claims.rationale: rerere.enabled turns recording on. The manual says to inspect with git diff before adding. The supplement recorded a resolution, aborted, and the next rebase applied Resolved 'base' using previous resolution. Applicability is hunk reuse, so a changed intent is not detected for the user.

claims.locator: TRANSPLANTING A TOPIC BRANCH WITH --ONTO: git rebase --onto master topicA topicB replays topicB commits that are not on topicA
claims.rationale: The second argument is the excluded upstream boundary, not the new base. The page's three-argument reading matches that diagram. The control left one commit on the transplanted branch.

claims.locator: Squash and merge combines the pull request into one commit; individual topic commits are not kept; the squash path uses the fast-forward option
claims.rationale: GitHub replaces the topic commits with one new commit, so the original base SHAs are not the commits on the default branch. The page describes that outcome. Local git merge --squash is a separate command and is not the GitHub button.

claims.locator: Revoke or rotate a secret first; clones, forks, cached SHA views, and pull requests can still expose it
claims.rationale: Rotation can be sufficient because a rewritten history does not prove the value was never copied. The page keeps interactive rebase on the unpublished branch and treats rewrite as one containment step.

claims.locator: fixup melds the change into the previous commit and discards the lower message; reflog and other refs are outside that branch update
claims.rationale: Folding the removal into the addition makes the surviving patch the net change. The six-commit run's inverted search found no super-secret-admin-pass. The reflog snapshot and the GitHub clone warning show that this does not clear every ref, reflog, or copy.

claims.locator: Updates since v1.7.3: git commit learned --fixup and --squash to help later interactive rebase
claims.rationale: The v1.7.4 notes record those options as preparation for interactive rebase. The page links the blob URL for this same v2.56.0 path; the catalog bytes are the raw file.

claims.locator: --expire defaults through gc.reflogExpire to 90 days; --expire-unreachable defaults through gc.reflogExpireUnreachable to 30 days
claims.rationale: Those are reflog-entry expiry defaults. The same section allows configuration and immediate pruning. Expiry of a reflog entry is not an object-retention guarantee.

claims.locator: Separate your changes: one logical change per patch; the tree should build and run after each patch so git bisect can split the series
claims.rationale: The guide asks for separate logical changes and a kernel that builds and runs after every patch because bisect can stop in the middle. The page's buildable-series wording matches that section.

claims.locator: ConfigMap caution: no secrecy or encryption; confidential data belongs in a Secret. Probe page configures liveness, readiness, and startup probes on the container
claims.rationale: The ConfigMap snapshot says confidential data belongs in a Secret. The Secrets snapshot is the confidential object. The probe snapshot documents liveness, readiness, and startup probes. The lab declares its manifests incomplete and not for a cluster. Additional snapshots: secrets sha256:595d1ee06d05430db8f7f83983d99813ad6bb1e59bb22a2a00f4fe69e340c08f and probes sha256:2a69b9a5354d355147f562bce0c808c875bb046b7b15b045f012c757c87fad7e.

claims.locator: DESCRIPTION keeps commits with no equivalent upstream commit; --empty drops clean cherry-picks from git log --cherry-mark unless --reapply-cherry-picks or --keep-base; patch IDs compare diff contents
claims.rationale: Plain rebase drops a commit when its patch matches an upstream commit. It does not compare commit ids alone. A multi-commit squash is one new patch and need not match each original patch. The Git 2.56.0 control replayed both database commits and conflicted, then --onto replayed only the API commit.

claims.locator: Splitting example: the untouched oldest pick stays unmodified because it was applied before any rewrite; reflog can still see the pre-rebase tip
claims.rationale: The book keeps f7f3f6d unchanged when a later commit is the one edited. The page's sometimes is that case, not a promise that every pick is reused. Old objects can remain through reflogs and other refs.

claims.locator: DESCRIPTION: after conflicts are resolved and staged, git rebase --continue resumes the still-running rebase
claims.rationale: The manual keeps the rebase in progress between add and continue. Git 2.56.0 printed interactive rebase in progress and all conflicts fixed: run git rebase --continue after the rerere resolution was staged.
